questions.text: What is the maximum power output (PEP) permitted for a UK Foundation licence holder?
questions.explanation: Foundation licence holders are limited to a maximum of 10 Watts PEP (Peak Envelope Power). Intermediate licence holders can use up to 50 Watts, and Full licence holders up to 400 Watts.

questions.text: What is the callsign prefix for a UK Foundation licence holder?
questions.explanation: UK Foundation licence holders are issued callsigns beginning with M7, followed by three letters (e.g., M7ABC). G0 and M0 are Full licence prefixes, and 2E0 is an Intermediate prefix.

questions.text: Which organisation regulates amateur radio in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: Ofcom (the Office of Communications) is the UK's independent communications regulator. They issue amateur radio licences and regulate spectrum use. The RSGB is the national society for amateur radio but does not regulate.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a condition of the UK amateur radio licence?
questions.explanation: Transmitting music is NOT permitted under the amateur radio licence. Licence holders must keep a log, identify their station by callsign, and operate within permitted bands.

questions.text: What suffix is added to a callsign when operating portable?
questions.explanation: /P indicates portable operation (from a temporary location). /M indicates mobile operation (from a vehicle), /A indicates alternative address, and /MM indicates maritime mobile.

questions.text: What is the Foundation callsign prefix used when operating from Scotland?
questions.explanation: MM7 is the prefix used by Foundation licence holders operating from Scotland. MW7 is for Wales, MI7 is for Northern Ireland, and M7 is for England.

questions.text: Under which Act is the UK amateur radio licence issued?
questions.explanation: The amateur radio licence is issued under the Wireless Telegraphy Act 2006, which governs the use of the radio spectrum in the UK.

questions.text: What is the minimum age to hold a UK Foundation amateur radio licence?
questions.explanation: There is no minimum age requirement for holding a UK amateur radio licence. People of any age can take the Foundation exam and obtain a licence.

questions.text: Which of the following must be recorded in your station logbook?

options.text: Date, time (UTC), frequency, mode, and callsign of station worked
Only the callsigns of stations worked
The serial number of your radio

questions.explanation: The logbook should record the date, time in UTC, frequency or band, mode of transmission, callsign of the station worked, and signal reports exchanged.

questions.text: How many licence levels are there in the UK amateur radio licensing system?
questions.explanation: There are three UK amateur radio licence levels: Foundation, Intermediate, and Full. Each progressive level requires passing an additional exam and grants higher power limits.

questions.text: What is the maximum power for a UK Full (Advanced) licence holder?
questions.explanation: Full licence holders can use up to 400 Watts PEP. Foundation is limited to 10W and Intermediate to 50W.

questions.text: Can an amateur radio licence be used for business communications?

options.text: Yes, but only during business hours
Yes, but only with Ofcom permission

questions.explanation: Amateur radio licences must not be used for business or commercial communications. Amateur radio is for personal experimentation, communication, and self-training.

questions.text: What does the Intermediate licence callsign prefix '2E0' indicate?

options.text: A Foundation licence holder in England
An Intermediate licence holder in England
A Full licence holder in England
A Foundation licence holder in Wales

questions.explanation: 2E0 is the callsign prefix for Intermediate licence holders in England. Foundation uses M7, and Full uses M0 or G-series prefixes.

questions.text: Are you permitted to transmit encrypted messages on amateur radio?

options.text: Generally no, except for certain control signals
Yes, but only on HF bands

questions.explanation: Generally, amateur transmissions must not be encrypted to hide their meaning. However, certain digital mode control signals and specific authorised applications may use encryption.

questions.text: What is the current cost of a UK amateur radio licence?
questions.explanation: UK amateur radio licences are currently issued free of charge by Ofcom. There is no annual fee.

questions.text: Using Ohm's Law, what is the current flowing through a 100Ω resistor connected to a 12V supply?
questions.explanation: Using Ohm's Law: I = V/R = 12/100 = 0.12 Amperes (120 milliamperes).

questions.text: What is the total resistance of three 100Ω resistors connected in series?
questions.explanation: Resistors in series add directly: R_total = R1 + R2 + R3 = 100 + 100 + 100 = 300Ω.

questions.text: What is the total resistance of two 100Ω resistors connected in parallel?
questions.explanation: For two equal resistors in parallel: R_total = R/2 = 100/2 = 50Ω. Using the formula: 1/R_total = 1/100 + 1/100 = 2/100, so R_total = 50Ω.

questions.text: A gain of +3 dB represents what change in power?
questions.explanation: +3 dB represents a doubling of power. This is one of the most important dB relationships to remember. -3 dB is half power, +10 dB is ten times power.

questions.text: What is the approximate wavelength of a signal at 145 MHz?
questions.explanation: Using λ = c/f: λ = 300,000,000 / 145,000,000 ≈ 2.07 metres. This is why 144-146 MHz is known as the '2 metre band'.

questions.text: What unit is used to measure electrical current?
questions.explanation: Current is measured in Amperes (Amps, A). Volts measure voltage, Ohms measure resistance, and Watts measure power.

questions.text: What formula relates power to voltage and current?
questions.explanation: Power (P) in Watts equals Voltage (V) in Volts multiplied by Current (I) in Amperes: P = V × I.

questions.text: What is the frequency of UK mains electricity?
questions.explanation: UK mains electricity runs at 50 Hz (50 cycles per second). In North America, the mains frequency is 60 Hz.

questions.text: What does a loss of -10 dB mean?

options.text: The power is reduced to one-half
The power is reduced to one-third
The power is reduced to one-tenth

questions.explanation: -10 dB means the power is reduced to one-tenth of its original level. +10 dB means ten times the power, -3 dB means half, +3 dB means double.

questions.text: What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength?
questions.explanation: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional: as frequency increases, wavelength decreases, and vice versa. The relationship is λ = c/f.

questions.text: What prefix represents one million?
questions.explanation: Mega (M) represents one million (10⁶). So 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz. Kilo is one thousand, Giga is one billion, milli is one-thousandth.

questions.text: What type of current flows from a battery?
questions.explanation: Batteries produce Direct Current (DC), which flows in one direction only. Alternating Current (AC) reverses direction periodically, as in mains electricity.

questions.text: What is the power dissipated in a 50Ω resistor when 2A of current flows through it?
questions.explanation: Using P = I² × R: P = 2² × 50 = 4 × 50 = 200 Watts.

questions.text: What is the voltage across a 25Ω resistor carrying 0.5A?
questions.explanation: Using Ohm's Law: V = I × R = 0.5 × 25 = 12.5 Volts.

questions.text: What is the approximate wavelength of a 7 MHz signal?
questions.explanation: λ = c/f = 300,000,000 / 7,000,000 ≈ 42.9 metres. This is why 7 MHz is known as the '40 metre band'.

questions.text: In a superheterodyne receiver, what is the purpose of the mixer?

options.text: To combine the received signal with the local oscillator to produce the IF

questions.explanation: The mixer combines the incoming RF signal with the local oscillator signal to produce the Intermediate Frequency (IF). This allows most of the amplification and selectivity to be provided at a fixed frequency.

questions.text: Which modulation type is most commonly used for HF voice communication?
questions.explanation: SSB (Single Sideband) is the most common mode for HF voice communication because it is much more efficient than AM in terms of both power and bandwidth. USB is used above 10 MHz, LSB below 10 MHz.

questions.text: What is the typical bandwidth of an SSB signal?
questions.explanation: An SSB signal has a typical bandwidth of about 2.4 kHz. Compare this with AM (6 kHz), narrow FM (12.5 kHz), and CW (500 Hz or less).

questions.text: What does FM stand for?
questions.explanation: FM stands for Frequency Modulation, where the frequency of the carrier wave is varied in accordance with the audio signal. FM is widely used on VHF and UHF bands.

questions.text: What is a transceiver?
questions.explanation: A transceiver is a device that combines both a transmitter and receiver in a single unit. Most modern amateur radio equipment is a transceiver.

questions.text: Which sideband is conventionally used for voice on frequencies above 10 MHz?
questions.explanation: By convention, USB (Upper Sideband) is used above 10 MHz and LSB (Lower Sideband) is used below 10 MHz for voice communications.

questions.text: What is the function of the demodulator in a receiver?

options.text: To amplify the radio frequency signal
To extract the original information from the IF signal
To generate the local oscillator frequency

questions.explanation: The demodulator (also called the detector) extracts the original audio or data information from the Intermediate Frequency signal, reversing the modulation process.

questions.text: What does receiver selectivity mean?

options.text: The ability to receive very weak signals
The ability to separate wanted signals from nearby unwanted signals
The maximum frequency range the receiver can tune
The audio output power of the receiver

questions.explanation: Selectivity is the ability of a receiver to select the wanted signal and reject nearby unwanted signals. It is primarily determined by the IF filter bandwidth.

questions.text: What does receiver sensitivity refer to?

options.text: How well it separates adjacent signals
Its ability to detect very weak signals

questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the ability of a receiver to detect weak signals. A more sensitive receiver can receive weaker signals, typically measured as the minimum discernible signal level.

questions.text: Which mode is used for VHF/UHF repeater communications?
questions.explanation: FM (Frequency Modulation) is the standard mode used for VHF and UHF repeater communications. It provides good audio quality and is more resistant to noise than AM.

questions.text: What is the purpose of the oscillator in a transmitter?

options.text: To generate a stable radio frequency signal
To amplify the signal to the desired power

questions.explanation: The oscillator generates a stable radio frequency (RF) signal at the desired operating frequency. This forms the basis of the transmitted signal.

questions.text: What is IF in a superheterodyne receiver?
questions.explanation: IF stands for Intermediate Frequency. It is a fixed frequency produced by the mixer, which allows the receiver to provide most of its gain and selectivity at this single frequency regardless of the tuned frequency.

questions.text: In AM, what part of the signal carries the information?
questions.explanation: In AM, the information is carried in the sidebands, not in the carrier. The carrier contains no information, which is why SSB (which removes the carrier) is more efficient.

questions.text: What does PTT stand for?
questions.explanation: PTT stands for Push To Talk. It is the switch (usually on the microphone) that switches the transceiver from receive mode to transmit mode.

questions.text: Which mode has the narrowest bandwidth?
questions.explanation: CW (Morse code) has the narrowest bandwidth at about 500 Hz or less. SSB uses about 2.4 kHz, AM about 6 kHz, and FM 12.5-25 kHz.

questions.text: What is the standard characteristic impedance of coaxial cable used in amateur radio?
questions.explanation: 50Ω is the standard impedance for amateur radio coaxial cable and equipment. 75Ω coax is used for television systems but not amateur radio.

questions.text: What does SWR stand for?
questions.explanation: SWR stands for Standing Wave Ratio. It measures how well the antenna impedance matches the feeder impedance. An SWR of 1:1 indicates a perfect match.

questions.text: What type of antenna radiates equally in all horizontal directions?
questions.explanation: A vertical (ground plane) antenna is omnidirectional — it radiates equally in all horizontal directions. A Yagi is directional, and a dipole radiates broadside to the wire.

questions.text: What is a balun used for?

options.text: To connect a balanced antenna to an unbalanced feeder

questions.explanation: A balun (balanced-to-unbalanced) connects a balanced antenna (such as a dipole) to an unbalanced feeder (such as coaxial cable). It prevents unwanted currents on the outer shield of the coax.

questions.text: What is the approximate feed point impedance of a half-wave dipole?
questions.explanation: A half-wave dipole has a feed point impedance of approximately 73Ω, which is close enough to 50Ω for a reasonable match to standard coaxial cable.

questions.text: What does an Antenna Tuning Unit (ATU) do?

options.text: Increases the gain of the antenna
Transforms the impedance to match the transmitter output

questions.explanation: An ATU transforms the impedance at the end of the feeder to match the transmitter's 50Ω output. It does NOT make the antenna more efficient — it simply provides a match so full power can be delivered.

questions.text: Which antenna type provides gain in a specific direction?
questions.explanation: The Yagi antenna is a directional antenna that provides gain in its forward direction. It has a driven element, a reflector behind it, and one or more directors in front.

questions.text: What SWR reading indicates a perfect match between feeder and antenna?
questions.explanation: An SWR of 1:1 indicates a perfect match. All power travels to the antenna with no reflected power. Higher ratios indicate increasingly poor matches.

questions.text: What happens when the SWR on a feeder is very high?

options.text: Power is reflected back to the transmitter and may cause damage

questions.explanation: High SWR means significant power is reflected back towards the transmitter. This wastes power and can potentially damage the transmitter's output stage.

questions.text: What is the polarisation of a vertical antenna?
questions.explanation: A vertical antenna produces vertically polarised signals. Vertical polarisation is commonly used for VHF/UHF FM communications.

questions.text: For best signal transfer, what polarisation should both stations use?
questions.explanation: Both stations should use the same polarisation for best signal transfer. A polarisation mismatch can result in significant signal loss of up to 20 dB.

questions.text: What is the total length of a half-wave dipole for the 2-metre band?
questions.explanation: A half-wave dipole for 2m is approximately 1 metre total length (half a wavelength). Each arm of the dipole is about 50cm.

questions.text: What determines the characteristic impedance of a coaxial cable?
questions.explanation: The characteristic impedance of coaxial cable is determined by the ratio of the diameters of the inner and outer conductors, and the dielectric material between them. It does not depend on length.

questions.text: Which coaxial cable type has lower signal loss?
questions.explanation: Thicker coaxial cable (like RG-213) has lower loss than thinner cable (like RG-58). This is because the larger conductors have lower resistance. Loss also increases with length and frequency.

questions.text: How many elements does a basic Yagi antenna have?

options.text: At least three (driven element, reflector, and one director)

questions.explanation: A basic Yagi has at least three elements: the driven element (connected to the feeder), a reflector behind it, and one or more directors in front. More directors give more gain.

questions.text: Which ionosphere layer is most important for long-distance HF communication?
questions.explanation: The F2 layer is the most important for HF long-distance communication. It is the highest layer (250-400 km) and is present both day and night, enabling worldwide communication.

questions.text: What happens to the D layer at night?

options.text: It merges with the F2 layer

questions.explanation: The D layer disappears at night because it depends on direct solar radiation. Since the D layer absorbs HF signals, its absence at night improves HF propagation, especially on lower frequencies.

questions.text: What is the MUF?
questions.explanation: MUF stands for Maximum Usable Frequency — the highest frequency that will be refracted back to Earth by the ionosphere for a given path. Above the MUF, signals pass through into space.

questions.text: VHF and UHF signals normally travel by which type of propagation?
questions.explanation: VHF and UHF signals normally travel by line of sight, similar to light. Range is typically limited to the visual horizon plus a small extension due to atmospheric refraction.

questions.text: What is skip distance?

options.text: The maximum range of a radio signal
The minimum distance at which sky wave signals return to Earth
The length of coaxial cable to the antenna

questions.explanation: Skip distance is the minimum distance from the transmitter at which sky wave signals return to Earth after reflection from the ionosphere. There is a 'dead zone' between ground wave and sky wave coverage.

questions.text: How can VHF range be increased?

options.text: By increasing antenna height and using directional antennas
By using AM instead of FM

questions.explanation: VHF range can be increased by raising antenna height (higher antennas see further over the horizon), using directional antennas for gain, and using repeaters on high ground.

questions.text: What is Sporadic E propagation?

options.text: Normal HF propagation via the F2 layer
Unpredictable VHF propagation caused by intense ionisation patches in the E layer

questions.explanation: Sporadic E occurs when patches of intense ionisation form in the E layer, reflecting VHF signals over hundreds of kilometres. It is unpredictable but can enable exciting long-distance VHF contacts.

questions.text: Approximately how long is the solar activity cycle?
questions.explanation: The solar cycle is approximately 11 years from one solar maximum to the next. During solar maximum, higher HF bands open up due to increased ionisation.

questions.text: What effect does the D layer have on HF signals?

options.text: It reflects them back to Earth
It absorbs them, especially at lower HF frequencies

questions.explanation: The D layer absorbs HF signals, particularly at lower HF frequencies. This is why daytime propagation on 80m and 40m is limited compared to night-time when the D layer disappears.

questions.text: Which of the following can cause unusual long-distance VHF propagation?
questions.explanation: Tropospheric ducting occurs when temperature inversions in the lower atmosphere guide VHF/UHF signals over much longer distances than normal. It is most common in summer with stable weather.

questions.text: At which type of solar condition do higher HF bands (10m, 15m) open for long-distance contacts?
questions.explanation: During solar maximum, increased solar radiation produces stronger ionisation, raising the MUF and opening higher HF bands (10m, 15m, 20m) for long-distance communication.

questions.text: What is ground wave propagation?

options.text: Signals that follow the curvature of the Earth's surface
Signals that travel in straight lines

questions.explanation: Ground wave propagation is where radio signals follow the surface of the Earth, bending around its curvature. It is most effective at lower frequencies (below about 2 MHz).

questions.text: What happens to a signal at a frequency above the MUF?

options.text: It is reflected back to Earth with extra strength
It passes through the ionosphere into space
It is absorbed by the D layer

questions.explanation: Signals above the Maximum Usable Frequency (MUF) pass through the ionosphere into space rather than being refracted back to Earth. This is why satellites can communicate through the ionosphere.

questions.text: At what height is the F2 layer of the ionosphere?
questions.explanation: The F2 layer is at approximately 250-400 km altitude. It is the highest regular ionospheric layer and the most important for HF radio propagation.

questions.text: Why is HF propagation often better at night on lower frequency bands?

options.text: There is less interference from other stations
The D layer, which absorbs lower HF signals, disappears at night
The antenna works better in the dark
The F2 layer also disappears at night

questions.explanation: The D layer, which absorbs lower HF signals during the day, disappears at night because it depends on solar radiation. This allows lower HF frequencies (80m, 40m) to reach the F2 layer and be reflected for long-distance contacts.

questions.text: What is breakthrough interference?

options.text: Interference caused by faulty antenna connections
Strong transmitted signals being picked up by nearby electronic equipment
A fault in the transmitter output stage

questions.explanation: Breakthrough occurs when strong signals from a nearby transmitter are picked up by consumer electronic equipment. The affected equipment cannot reject the strong radio signal.

questions.text: What is a harmonic?

options.text: A signal at a multiple of the fundamental frequency

questions.explanation: A harmonic is a signal at a whole-number multiple of the fundamental (operating) frequency. The 2nd harmonic of 7 MHz is 14 MHz, the 3rd harmonic is 21 MHz, etc.

questions.text: What type of filter should be used on a transmitter output to reduce harmonics?
questions.explanation: A low-pass filter on the transmitter output allows the wanted signal through but blocks higher-frequency harmonics. This is one of the most effective measures for reducing harmonic interference.

questions.text: What is the first thing you should do if a neighbour complains about interference?

options.text: Be polite and investigate whether it is caused by your station
Increase your power to overcome the problem

questions.explanation: Always be polite and cooperative. First establish whether the interference is actually from your station by stopping transmitting and asking if the problem stops. Good neighbour relations are essential.

questions.text: What can be fitted to the leads of affected equipment to reduce breakthrough?
questions.explanation: Ferrite chokes (clip-on ferrites) fitted to the cables of affected equipment can block RF energy from entering the equipment, preventing breakthrough interference.

questions.text: How can you help minimise EMC problems at your own station?

options.text: Use maximum power at all times
Use minimum necessary power and maintain good SWR
Use as many antennas as possible

questions.explanation: Using minimum power reduces the chance of causing breakthrough. Good SWR ensures the antenna system is efficient and not radiating from the feeder. These are fundamental good EMC practices.

questions.text: What is the 2nd harmonic of a 14 MHz transmission?
questions.explanation: The 2nd harmonic is twice the fundamental frequency: 2 × 14 MHz = 28 MHz. The 3rd harmonic would be 3 × 14 = 42 MHz.

questions.text: Which organisation can you contact for EMC advice?
questions.explanation: The RSGB (Radio Society of Great Britain) has an EMC Committee that provides advice and assistance to amateur radio operators dealing with electromagnetic compatibility issues.

questions.text: What does QRM mean?
questions.explanation: QRM refers to man-made interference (from other stations, electrical equipment, etc.). QRN refers to natural noise (static from thunderstorms, etc.).

questions.text: Why is maintaining good SWR important for reducing interference?

options.text: It ensures the feeder doesn't radiate and cause unwanted interference
It makes the antenna spin faster
It increases the frequency of transmission

questions.explanation: Good SWR means the feeder is properly matched and doesn't itself become an antenna. A poorly matched feeder can radiate RF energy close to your house and neighbours' equipment, causing interference.

questions.text: What might cause interference to your own receiver?

options.text: Switch-mode power supplies and LED lighting

questions.explanation: Your receiver can suffer interference from switch-mode power supplies, LED lighting, PLT/BPL devices, and also from other amateur or commercial radio transmissions.

questions.text: What is the purpose of screening in electronic equipment?

options.text: To make the equipment look better
To prevent RF energy from entering or leaving the equipment

questions.explanation: Screening (shielding) using metal enclosures prevents unwanted RF energy from entering the equipment (causing interference) or from leaving it (causing emissions). It is a fundamental EMC technique.

questions.text: When should you NOT transmit to help identify an interference source?

options.text: When a neighbour reports interference — stop to see if the problem stops

questions.explanation: When investigating an interference complaint, stop transmitting to see if the problem stops. This helps confirm whether your station is the source of the interference.

questions.text: What type of filter should be fitted to a TV aerial lead to reduce amateur radio interference?
questions.explanation: A high-pass filter on a TV aerial lead allows the higher TV frequencies through while blocking the lower amateur radio frequencies that might cause breakthrough.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a good EMC practice?

options.text: Using the longest possible coax runs

questions.explanation: Using unnecessarily long coax runs increases signal loss and can increase the chance of the feeder picking up or radiating interference. Good practice is to keep feeders as short as practical.

questions.text: What is the phonetic alphabet word for the letter 'G'?
questions.explanation: In the NATO/ICAO phonetic alphabet, 'G' is 'Golf'. This standardised alphabet is used to avoid confusion when spelling callsigns over the air.

questions.text: What does the Q-code 'QTH' mean?
questions.explanation: QTH means 'What is your location?' (as a question) or 'My location is...' (as a statement). It is one of the most commonly used Q-codes in amateur radio.

questions.text: In the RST system, what does a signal report of '59' mean?
questions.explanation: R5 = perfectly readable, S9 = extremely strong signal. A report of 59 is the best possible signal report for a phone (voice) contact.

questions.text: What does CTCSS stand for?
questions.explanation: CTCSS stands for Continuous Tone-Coded Squelch System. It is a low-frequency sub-audible tone transmitted along with your voice that opens the squelch on a repeater.

questions.text: What is the difference between simplex and duplex operation?

options.text: Simplex uses AM, duplex uses FM
Simplex transmits and receives on the same frequency, duplex uses different frequencies
Simplex is for CW only, duplex is for voice

questions.explanation: Simplex means transmitting and receiving on the same frequency. Duplex means using different frequencies for transmit and receive, as used with repeaters.

questions.text: What does 'CQ' mean when transmitted?

options.text: General call inviting any station to respond

questions.explanation: CQ is a general call inviting any station to respond. It is used when you want to make a contact with anyone who is listening.

questions.text: What does '73' mean in amateur radio?
questions.explanation: 73 means 'best wishes' and is used to end a contact. It is singular — you say '73', not 'seventy-threes'.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a repeater?

options.text: To receive signals on one frequency and retransmit them on another, extending range

questions.explanation: A repeater receives signals on its input frequency and simultaneously retransmits them on its output frequency, typically from a high location, greatly extending the range of low-power stations.

questions.text: What is the standard frequency shift for a 2-metre repeater?
questions.explanation: The standard repeater shift on the 2-metre band is 600 kHz. On 70cm, the shift is 1.6 MHz.

questions.text: What does QRZ mean?
questions.explanation: QRZ means 'Who is calling me?' It is used when you hear someone calling but didn't catch their callsign. It can also be used as a general enquiry to see if anyone is calling.

questions.text: What does QSY mean?
questions.explanation: QSY means 'Change frequency to...' or as a question 'Shall I change frequency?' It is used to move a conversation to a different frequency.

questions.text: Which word should you use at the end of your transmission when you expect a reply?
questions.explanation: 'Over' means you have finished speaking and expect a reply. 'Out' means you have finished and do NOT expect a reply (end of contact). Never say 'over and out' — they are contradictory!

questions.text: What is the 2-metre FM calling frequency?
questions.explanation: 145.500 MHz is the 2-metre FM calling frequency. After making initial contact on the calling frequency, stations should QSY to another frequency to continue their conversation.

questions.text: What does QSL mean?

options.text: I acknowledge receipt / Can you confirm?

questions.explanation: QSL means 'I acknowledge receipt' (as a statement) or 'Can you acknowledge receipt?' (as a question). QSL cards are postcards exchanged between stations to confirm a contact.

questions.text: What does QRN refer to?
questions.explanation: QRN refers to natural noise, including static from thunderstorms and atmospheric disturbances. Compare with QRM which refers to man-made interference.

questions.text: What is the voltage of UK mains electricity?
questions.explanation: UK mains electricity is nominally 230V AC at 50 Hz. This is a potentially lethal voltage and must be treated with great respect.

questions.text: What should you do FIRST if someone is receiving an electric shock?

options.text: Grab them and pull them away
Switch off the power supply or separate them using a non-conducting object

questions.explanation: NEVER touch a person who is still in contact with a live electrical source. First switch off the supply, or use a non-conducting object (dry wood, plastic) to separate them from the source.

questions.text: What is the greatest danger with antennas?
questions.explanation: Contact with overhead power lines is the greatest danger associated with antennas. This is extremely dangerous and frequently fatal. Always ensure antennas are erected well away from power lines.

questions.text: What should you do with your antenna during a thunderstorm?

options.text: Disconnect it from the equipment and earth the feeder
Leave it connected but stop transmitting

questions.explanation: During thunderstorms, disconnect the antenna from your equipment and earth the feeder. Do not operate during thunderstorms. Lightning can induce dangerous voltages in antenna systems.

questions.text: What emergency number should you call if someone receives a serious electric shock?
questions.explanation: Call 999 (or 112, the European emergency number) for serious electric shock. This is a medical emergency requiring immediate professional help.

questions.text: Why should you keep RF antennas away from people?

options.text: RF energy can cause heating of body tissues
The antenna might fall on them

questions.explanation: RF energy can cause heating of body tissues, particularly at higher power levels and frequencies. Antennas should be mounted high enough that people are not exposed to strong RF fields.

questions.text: What is the purpose of a fuse?

options.text: To protect the circuit by breaking when excessive current flows

questions.explanation: A fuse protects a circuit by melting and breaking the circuit when the current exceeds a safe level. This prevents damage to equipment and reduces fire risk.

questions.text: What should you do before working inside any electrical equipment?

options.text: Switch off and unplug the equipment

questions.explanation: Always switch off and unplug equipment before working inside it. Some equipment, particularly valve amplifiers, may have charged capacitors that remain dangerous even after switching off.

questions.text: What is an RCD (Residual Current Device)?

options.text: A safety device that quickly disconnects the supply if current leaks to earth

questions.explanation: An RCD detects current leaking to earth (which could be through a person) and rapidly disconnects the mains supply. It provides additional protection against electric shock.

questions.text: What position should you place an unconscious but breathing person in?
questions.explanation: An unconscious but breathing person should be placed in the recovery position. This keeps their airway clear and allows any fluids to drain from the mouth.

questions.text: What danger exists in valve (tube) amplifiers even after they are switched off?

options.text: Capacitors may retain a lethal charge

questions.explanation: Capacitors in valve amplifiers can retain a lethal high-voltage charge for a considerable time after the equipment is switched off. They must be safely discharged before any work is carried out.

questions.text: What does PAT stand for in the context of electrical safety?
questions.explanation: PAT stands for Portable Appliance Testing — the inspection and testing of electrical equipment to ensure it is safe to use. It involves visual checks and basic electrical measurements.

questions.text: Which of the following is the safest approach regarding transmitter power?

options.text: Use the minimum power necessary for the contact
Use exactly half your maximum power

questions.explanation: Using the minimum power necessary reduces RF exposure to people nearby, reduces the risk of interference to other equipment, and is a licence condition. It is both safer and good operating practice.

questions.text: What should be used to separate a person from a live electrical source if you cannot switch off the power?

options.text: A dry non-conducting object like wood or plastic

questions.explanation: Use a dry, non-conducting object such as a wooden broom handle, dry clothing, or plastic object. Never use metal, wet objects, or your bare hands to separate someone from a live electrical source.

questions.text: Why is proper earthing of radio equipment important?

options.text: It provides a safety path for fault currents, protecting the operator from electric shock
It is only needed for portable operation

questions.explanation: Proper earthing provides a low-resistance path for fault currents to flow safely to earth, tripping the fuse or RCD. Without it, the equipment case could become live, putting the operator at risk of electric shock.
